title: RBI Deposit Drive Attracts $73 Billion in NRI Inflows in Just 11 Weeks
excerpt: India's central bank closed its special FCNR(B) swap window a month early after foreign currency deposits surpassed all expectations.
body:
• India attracted $73 billion in foreign exchange in 11 weeks through a special RBI deposit scheme for NRIs
  • FCNR(B) deposits contributed $65.4 billion, with additional inflows from overseas borrowings
  • The RBI closed the swap window a month early on August 31, having exceeded its objectives
  • The current program dwarfs the 2013 effort, which raised $26 billion over roughly three months

India has attracted $73 billion in foreign exchange in just 11 weeks, marking one of the fastest foreign-currency fundraising efforts in its history and far exceeding the Reserve Bank of India's own targets. The inflows were driven primarily by a special deposit scheme designed for Non-Resident Indians that offered unusually attractive returns.

How the Scheme Worked

The RBI introduced the program on June 5, 2026, to strengthen India's foreign exchange reserves and support the rupee during a period of global financial uncertainty linked to the US-Iran conflict and broader geopolitical instability. Under the scheme, the central bank offered banks a special USD-INR forex swap facility covering Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposits, external commercial borrowings and overseas foreign currency borrowings.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=FANrC9T1kyM

The favorable swap rate allowed banks to pass on higher returns to NRI depositors, offering interest rates of 6 to 7.5 percent on FCNR(B) deposits of three to five years' duration. Because these deposits remain in foreign currency, NRIs could earn interest without rupee exposure, a major incentive during periods of global volatility.

"The most likely reason for early closure could be that the target for FCNR(B) mobilization has already been achieved."

— Saumya Kanti Ghosh, Group Chief Economic Advisor, SBI

The Numbers

According to RBI data through August 21, FCNR(B) deposits contributed $65.4 billion of the total inflows. Overseas foreign currency borrowings added around $4.9 billion, with external commercial borrowings contributing roughly $2.6 billion, bringing total inflows under the special framework to approximately $72.8 billion, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

Banks mobilized $13.1 billion in the eight days ending August 21 alone. Market experts had projected total inflows could reach $80 billion before the window closed. The response was so strong that the RBI decided to close the FCNR(B) swap window one month early, ending it on August 31 instead of the originally planned September 30.

Why It Matters for NRIs

The scheme has been far larger than India's previous comparable effort. In 2013, the RBI raised about $26 billion over roughly three months through a similar FCNR(B) initiative during the taper tantrum. The current program has surpassed both the size and speed of that earlier effort nearly threefold.

For NRIs, the scheme offered a rare window to park foreign-currency savings in Indian banks at elevated interest rates without taking on currency risk. Axis Bank CEO Amitabh Chaudhry told Bloomberg that banks would likely use the fresh funds to replace expensive domestic deposits before deploying capital into infrastructure projects, data-center investments and commercial real estate.

Economic Impact

Economists say the inflows will help India maintain healthy foreign exchange reserves and improve confidence in the country's financial markets. Larger reserves give the RBI more flexibility to manage currency volatility if global conditions deteriorate further. The reserves also provide a buffer against potential capital outflows during the ongoing geopolitical tensions in West Asia.
